analysis.one_liner: Ends tax breaks, royalty relief, and federal financing subsidies for oil, gas, and coal companies.
analysis.headline: A bill to strip federal subsidies from oil, gas, and coal companies never got a hearing or vote; it died after referral to nine House committees in the 112th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end a wide range of federal support for fossil fuel companies: tax breaks like the oil depletion allowance and credits for producing from marginal wells, royalty relief on offshore oil and gas leases, taxpayer-funded research through the Energy Department's fossil energy office, export financing for overseas coal and oil projects, and loan guarantees for advanced fossil technology and refineries. It would also raise federal royalty rates on coal, oil, and gas from 12.5% to 18.75%, impose a 13% tax on Gulf of Mexico offshore production, and remove the cap on what companies must pay after an oil spill.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would stop funding billions in tax breaks and research for profitable energy companies; coastal communities and public treasuries, which would be fully compensated after oil spills instead of only up to a legal cap; and federal, state, and local governments collecting higher royalties.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Interior Secretary's authority to reduce or eliminate royalty payments on Outer Continental Shelf oil and gas leases, and bars any future royalty relief under such leases.
It raises the minimum federal royalty on coal, oil, and natural gas leases on federal land from 12.5% to 18.75%, meaning more of the value of publicly owned resources flows to the government.

It removes the liability cap under the Oil Pollution Act for offshore facilities and pipeline operators, so companies responsible for a spill would owe the full cleanup and damage costs rather than a capped amount.

It terminates more than a dozen tax provisions benefiting fossil fuel companies, including the enhanced oil recovery credit, percentage depletion for oil, gas, and coal wells, and the domestic manufacturing deduction for oil, gas, coal, and hard mineral production.

It rescinds unspent federal funds at the World Bank, the Overseas Private Investment Corporation, and the Export-Import Bank for coal, oil, and natural gas projects, and bars future use of those funds for such projects.
It eliminates the Energy Department's Office of Fossil Energy Research and Development and removes advanced fossil energy projects and refineries from eligibility for federal loan guarantees.
The bill's findings cite research showing federal fossil fuel subsidies of over $72 billion from 2002 through 2008, more than five times federal renewable energy investments in the same period.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal companies, which would pay higher taxes, higher royalties on federal land, a new 13% tax on Gulf of Mexico offshore production, and unlimited oil spill liability. Some of those costs could be passed through to consumers in energy prices.

drawbacks.text: Higher royalties, a new 13% offshore production tax, and repealed tax breaks would raise production costs for fossil fuels, and companies could pass some of those costs to consumers through higher prices.
Eliminating credits for producing oil and gas from marginal wells could push small, low-margin producers out of business and reduce domestic production.

The bill shuts down the Energy Department's entire fossil energy research office and bars federal agencies from financing any coal, oil, or gas project, which would cut off research and demonstration spending on cleaner uses of fossil fuels, such as carbon capture, along with subsidies for production.
Removing the liability cap on offshore facilities and pipelines would raise insurance and compliance costs across the industry, not just for companies with poor safety records.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: taxpayers and governments would stop underwriting some of the most profitable companies in the country, and spill victims would be made whole, at the price of modestly higher energy production costs that could reach consumers. The bill is aggressive in scope — it ends not only production subsidies but all federal fossil energy research and financing — so some provisions, like eliminating carbon capture research funding, go beyond ending giveaways to companies and cut programs with broader purposes. Still, the bill's main effect is to shift the cost of fossil fuel production from the public to the companies profiting from it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to nine House committees and a series of their subcommittees, but none of them ever acted on it, and it never came up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the End Polluter Welfare Act of 2012 on May 15, 2012, with three Democratic cosponsors.
The House referred the bill to nine committees, including Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, and Financial Services, with no single committee given clear lead responsibility.

Over the following two months, the bill was referred to seven subcommittees, including subcommittees on Energy and Power, Energy and Mineral Resources, and Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials; the last referral was on July 11, 2012.
No committee ever reported the bill, and no floor vote ever took place before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal companies, which kept the tax breaks, royalty relief, liability caps, and federal financing the bill would have taken away. Taxpayers continued paying for those supports.

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to eliminate fossil fuel subsidies and organized its referral in the House.

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Joined G20 leaders in pledging to phase out fossil fuel subsidies and repeatedly proposed eliminating oil and gas tax breaks in his budgets, lending political support to the bill's goal.

against.name: House committee chairs (9 committees)
against.role: Chairs of the committees the bill was referred to, including Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill; the record shows only referrals to committees and subcommittees, with no action reported back.

against.name: John Boehner
against.what_they_did: As Speaker, controlled which bills reached the floor; the bill never received a vote during the remainder of the 112th Congress.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against efforts in 2011 and 2012 to repeal oil and gas tax breaks and raise royalties, framing them as tax increases that would raise fuel prices.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill sat untouched in committees chaired by Republicans in a Republican-controlled House; no Republican support appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill would end their royalty relief on offshore leases, raise federal royalties from 12.5% to 18.75%, repeal over a dozen tax breaks, add a 13% tax on Gulf of Mexico production, and remove the cap on oil spill liability. These are all costs the companies have avoided at public expense, so their interest in keeping them runs against taxpayers and spill victims.

The bill would raise coal lease royalties, repeal percentage depletion and capital gains treatment for coal royalties, deny them the domestic manufacturing deduction, and cut off federal export financing and World Bank funding for coal projects. The public currently absorbs costs the companies would otherwise bear.

industries.industry: Rural electric utilities using fossil fuels
industries.note: The bill would bar the Rural Utilities Service from making loans for any project that uses coal, oil, or natural gas, ending a source of federally backed financing for rural power projects.

By ending tens of billions in cumulative fossil fuel support, the bill would shift the competitive balance toward renewable energy sources that would no longer be underfunded relative to fossil fuels. The bill does not directly subsidize renewables; it removes the disadvantage.
